details:
NEXANALOG – Project Description

NEXANALOG is an interactive scientific platform designed to explore, analyze, and compare the surfaces of Earth, Mars, and the Moon using advanced 3D geospatial visualization. Its main purpose is to identify terrestrial locations that have similar topographic characteristics to selected regions on other planetary bodies, helping researchers find suitable analog sites for testing equipment and preparing future space exploration missions.

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

NEXANALOG collects and processes real, open-access elevation data from NASA and other scientific agencies, including SRTM, ArcticDEM, MOLA MEGDR, and LRO LOLA. It analyzes four main topographic variables: average elevation, slope, terrain roughness, and local relief.

The platform uses an Analog Compatibility Index (ACI), which assigns a similarity score from 0 to 100 to compare terrestrial regions with selected locations on Mars and the Moon. Users can explore three-dimensional planetary globes, select specific regions, visualize terrain characteristics, and compare two locations side by side. It also displays data coverage, interpolation levels, and resolution limitations to ensure transparency in the results.

2. What benefits does it offer?

NEXANALOG makes complex planetary and geospatial information easier to understand through an interactive and accessible interface. It allows users to compare different environments using consistent topographic measurements instead of relying only on visual observations.

It can help identify potential terrestrial analog sites, support scientific research, assist in planning equipment tests, and provide a useful starting point for evaluating environments relevant to future lunar and Martian missions.

3. What is the expected impact of the project?

The expected impact is to contribute to planetary exploration research by improving the identification and preliminary evaluation of terrestrial analog environments. Locations such as the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley, and the Salar de Uyuni can be analyzed and compared with regions such as Jezero Crater and lunar sites.

By making scientific data more accessible and comparisons more transparent, NEXANALOG aims to support students, researchers, and future engineering teams in understanding planetary environments and preparing for exploration beyond Earth.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

The project uses React and Vite for the frontend structure, while Three.js and WebGL provide the interactive 3D visualization of planetary surfaces. Its geospatial data system is organized through a validated data manifest and a versioned API (/api/v1), which centralizes datasets, coordinate reference systems, and calculated terrain metrics.

The main scientific data sources include NASA SRTM, ArcticDEM, NASA PDS MOLA MEGDR, and NASA PDS LRO LOLA. Development and testing are performed using computer-based software tools, with no specialized physical hardware required for the platform itself.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

NEXANALOG combines planetary science, geospatial analysis, and interactive 3D technology into a single platform. Instead of simply displaying planetary images, it transforms real elevation data into measurable terrain characteristics and automatically calculates similarities between different worlds.

Its innovative approach includes a customizable comparison system, synchronized planetary views, interactive terrain layers, and transparent data-quality indicators. This allows users not only to see how two locations compare but also to understand which characteristics contribute to their similarity.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The team considered several important factors when developing the project:

  • Scientific accuracy: Using real datasets from recognized space agencies and respecting their coordinate reference systems.
  • Terrain characteristics: Comparing elevation, slope, roughness, and local relief.
  • Data quality: Identifying missing, interpolated, and directly measured elevation cells.
  • Sensor resolution: Considering differences between the spatial resolutions of terrestrial, Martian, and lunar datasets.
  • Accessibility: Designing an intuitive interface that allows users to explore complex information without requiring advanced geospatial knowledge.
  • Scientific limitations: Clearly communicating that the ACI measures topographic similarity only and does not independently establish geological composition, resource availability, or landing safety.

Ultimately, NEXANALOG aims to connect planetary science with practical engineering by providing a visual, measurable, and transparent way to discover and evaluate potential analog environments on Earth.
